summary: An answer key now checks the Employer stock page: 1,500 vesting schedules and 2,500 made-up households worked from the tax law and IRS publications, never from the app's code. After four fixes the page agrees with it on every row. The biggest: selling company shares at a loss now lowers this year's tax instead of counting as zero.
points: A sale at a loss first cancels the year's other gains, then comes off other income up to $3,000 a year ($1,500 each when filing separately), and the rest carries to later years.
Filing separately, the state's share of the vests starts from the employee's own return, so a spouse's pay no longer uses up the employee's state exemption.
With nothing staked in the company, the page explains how to start instead of calling it "a large bet on one company".

When a year's federal tax tables are not out yet (2027 today), the page says that year's figures are an estimate; with no pay from the employer on file, it says the 22% withholding assumes the employer already withholds from pay.
It also found that Illinois's 2026 exemption is $2,925, not $2,850; that figure belongs to the State income tax page, so it was passed to the other session.
numbers: 243 of 1,549 sales had too much tax shown (by up to $1,110)
A $45,000 loss on $40,000 of pay: about $360 less tax this year, $42,000 carried over

shots.caption: A sample household selling company shares bought higher: a $42,000 loss lowers this year's federal tax by about $360, and $39,000 carries to later years. Above it, the notes on the 22% and on 2027's tables.
With no shares and no grants, the page now says how to start instead of calling it a bet.
